title: The Magellanic Clouds
subtitle: Our neighbor galaxies
yt_title: Two Galaxies You Can See With Your Eyes 🌌 | Ep. 116 #shorts
description:
Episode 116 of a daily journey through the universe. 🌌
We visit the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds: galaxies about 160,000 and 200,000 light-years away, visible to the naked eye from the Southern Hemisphere, the Tarantula Nebula, Supernova 1987A, and a collision with the Milky Way in about 2 billion years.

➡️ Tomorrow, Episode 117: Next stop, globular clusters. Ancient balls of a million stars.
Start from Episode 1 "Leaving Earth" on the channel.
Follow so you don't miss a stop. A new episode every day.

segments.text: Episode one hundred and sixteen. Next stop... the Magellanic Clouds.
From the Southern Hemisphere, on a dark night, you can see two faint clouds in the sky. They're not clouds. They're galaxies.
segments.headline: Two clouds that are galaxies

segments.text: The Large Magellanic Cloud is about one hundred and sixty thousand light-years away.
The Small one is about two hundred thousand light-years away.
They're named after the explorer Ferdinand Magellan, whose crew described them in the fifteen hundreds. People in the south knew them for thousands of years before.
segments.headline: Known for millennia

segments.text: The Large Cloud holds the Tarantula Nebula, the biggest star factory in our neighborhood.
segments.headline: The Tarantula Nebula

segments.text: In nineteen eighty-seven, a star there exploded. The closest supernova seen in almost four hundred years.
segments.headline: Supernova 1987A

segments.text: The Large Cloud is surprisingly heavy, maybe a tenth of the Milky Way's mass.
segments.headline: A heavy neighbor

segments.text: In about two billion years, it's expected to crash into the Milky Way.
Tomorrow, glittering balls of a million stars, some of the oldest things in our galaxy. Follow, so you don't miss episode one hundred and seventeen.
